title: Pointers: variables that hold addresses
objective: By the end of this lesson you can read any pointer declaration, use & and * correctly, and explain what a pointer actually contains — which is simpler than its reputation suggests.

blocks.text: Every variable lives at an address in memory. A pointer is a variable whose value is one of those addresses. That is the entire concept. The difficulty people report is almost always about the notation, not the idea.

blocks.caption: The two operators
lines: int *p = &x;        /* & takes the address of x; p now holds it */
printf("%p\n", (void *)p);   /* the same address — that is what p holds */
printf("%d\n", *p);    /* 42  — * follows the address back to the value */
printf("%d\n", x);     /* 99 — x changed, because p pointed at it */

rows: the value at the address in p
p is a pointer to an int
make p hold the address of x
store 5 at the address p holds

blocks.title: The asterisk means two different things
blocks.text: In a declaration, int *p means 'p is a pointer to int'. In an expression, *p means 'the value at p'. Same symbol, opposite directions — declaration describes the type, expression performs the lookup. Reading declarations right to left helps: int *p is 'p is a pointer to int'.

blocks.caption: The type says how much to read and how far to step
lines: int    *pi;    /* reading *pi reads 4 bytes and interprets them as an int */
/* All three hold an address of the same size.
The type is not about the pointer — it is about what happens when you follow it. */

blocks.text: NULL: a pointer that points at nothing

blocks.caption: The convention, and the check
lines: printf("%d\n", *p);     /* only follow it after checking */
int *q;                     /* UNINITIALISED — not NULL, holds garbage */
*q = 5;                     /* undefined behaviour: writes to an unknown address */
int *r = NULL;              /* always initialise, even to NULL */

blocks.title: An uninitialised pointer is more dangerous than a NULL one
blocks.text: Dereferencing NULL usually crashes immediately, which is loud and easy to find. An uninitialised pointer holds whatever bytes were left on the stack, which may be a valid-looking address — so the write succeeds and quietly corrupts something else. Initialise every pointer at declaration, even if only to NULL.
The main reason pointers exist: letting a function change your variable

blocks.caption: Output parameters
lines: get_dimensions(&w, &h);       /* pass addresses so the function can write back */
int divide(int a, int b, int *result) {   /* status plus an output value */

blocks.text: const and pointers: three different promises

blocks.caption: Read the declaration right to left
lines: const char *p;        /* pointer to const char: cannot change *p, can change p */
char *const p;        /* const pointer to char: can change *p, cannot change p */
const char *const p;  /* neither can change */
void print(const char *text);   /* promises not to modify what text points at */

blocks.title: const in a parameter is documentation the compiler enforces
blocks.text: A function taking const char * is telling every caller that the data will not be modified, and the compiler will reject any attempt inside the function. It costs nothing and removes a question the reader would otherwise have to answer by reading the whole body.

blocks.caption: One more level, same rules
lines: int **pp = &p;        /* pp holds the address of p */
/* Used when a function must change the caller's pointer: */
allocate(&data);       /* without the extra level, data would stay NULL */

blocks.title: See addresses and values side by side
steps: Run: *p = 99; then print x — confirm it changed
Declare int *q = NULL; and print it with %p
Write get_dimensions(int *, int *) and call it with &w, &h
Add const char *name = "fixed"; then try name[0] = 'F'; and read the compile error
Write allocate(int **out) and confirm data is non-NULL after the call
blocks.expected: The same address printed two ways, a value changed through a pointer, a function writing into your variables, a const violation caught at compile time, and a pointer-to-pointer that lets a function replace your pointer. Nothing here is conceptually hard — it is all one idea seen from several angles.

cheatsheet: A pointer holds an address; that is the whole concept
&x = the address of x · *p = the value at p
In a declaration * marks the type; in an expression * performs the lookup
The pointer's type decides how many bytes are read when you follow it
Initialise every pointer, even to NULL — an uninitialised pointer may look valid and corrupt memory
Pass &variable so a function can write back to it
const char *p protects the data; char *const p protects the pointer
int **pp is used when a function must change the caller's pointer itself

checkpoint.prompt: What does a pointer variable actually contain?

choices.A: A copy of the value it points to
choices.D: A reference counted by the runtime

checkpoint.explanation: That is all it is. The type attached to it decides how the memory at that address is interpreted when you follow it.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is an uninitialised pointer more dangerous than a NULL one?

choices.A: It is not — both crash the same way
choices.B: NULL usually crashes immediately and loudly; an uninitialised pointer may hold a plausible address, so the write succeeds and quietly corrupts something else

checkpoint.explanation: A loud failure is a good failure. Silent corruption surfaces later, somewhere unrelated, and is far harder to trace.

checkpoint.prompt: You want a function to set two of the caller's variables. How?

choices.B: Take pointers to them and write through those pointers

checkpoint.explanation: C passes by value and can return only one thing, so output parameters are the standard mechanism.

choices.B: The characters p points to will not be modified through p — though p itself may be reassigned
choices.C: Both the pointer and the data are fixed
choices.D: The string is stored in read-only memory
